title: CIR and Lognormal Short-Rate Models

maps.tested: Named as a standalone must-do item by two sheets and reported once as a solved numerical.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'CIR model solving'. CIR: mean-reverting, basis-point volatility proportional to sqrt(r), rates cannot go negative. Lognormal with deterministic drift: volatility proportional to r. This three-way set against Vasicek (mean-reverting, can go negative) and Ho-Lee (no mean reversion, normal) is the highest-yield sibling swap in Market Risk.

vardeezReading: MR-15: Very Important; his pointers are the CIR model, the concept of terminal distributions, Model 3 and the lognormal model with deterministic drift (understand the interpretation). MR-14: Very Important; "Calculations are super important here" (Vasicek calculation, Ho-Lee model, expected rate in 7 years).

los.vardeez: CIR model; concept of terminal distributions
Lognormal model with deterministic drift: understand interpretation

selectors.name: CIR one-step rate change
selectors.what: One step of the CIR short-rate change from the drift, the volatility and a given random draw: delta r = k(theta - r) dt + sigma x sqrt(r) x z x sqrt(dt), then the new rate.
selectors.theory: The drift term is not random and scales with dt; the random term scales with sqrt(dt) because the standard deviation of dw is sqrt(dt). Mean reversion pulls the rate toward theta at speed k; forgetting dt on the drift or sqrt(dt) on the shock are separate errors.

selectors.name: CIR basis-point volatility versus sigma
selectors.what: In CIR the basis-point volatility is sigma x sqrt(r), not the constant parameter sigma (sigma = 0.05 at r = 3.6% gives about 95 bp, not 500 bp). Also calibrating sigma to a common basis-point volatility: sigma_CIR = sigma_bp / sqrt(r*) (0.0354 for 100 bp at 8%), against sigma_Y = sigma_bp / r* = 12.5% for the proportional form.
selectors.theory: Sigma is constant but basis-point volatility is not: it rises with the square root of the rate level and is zero at a zero rate, so CIR and proportional volatility both rise with the rate but at different speeds.

selectors.name: Non-negativity: CIR and lognormal versus normal
selectors.what: Which models can produce negative rates and why: CIR (volatility falls to zero at a zero rate, drift is positive there) and lognormal models (multiplicative shocks, e^x > 0) cannot; normal models (Ho-Lee, Vasicek) can. Includes the methods for negative rates: change the distribution or set negative tree rates to zero, and the claim that CIR is always the better model, which is false.

selectors.name: Lognormal models, volatility proportional to r
selectors.what: Lognormal short-rate models: basis-point volatility is sigma x r, with sigma the yield volatility (constant percentage of the rate), under deterministic drift (Model 4, Salomon Brothers: dr = a(t) r dt + sigma r dw) or mean reversion (Courtadon, Black-Karasinski). Separates deterministic drift from mean reversion in the log rate.
selectors.theory: By Ito's lemma d ln r = (a(t) - sigma^2 / 2) dt + sigma dw, so ln r is normal and r is lognormal; the tree nodes r0 x e^(a dt +/- sigma sqrt(dt)) are all positive and the up node is about r0 x (1 + sigma), so a 12.5% yield volatility moves the rate about 12.5% of its level. Salomon Brothers is the Ho-Lee model on ln r; Black-Karasinski is a time-dependent Vasicek process on ln r.

selectors.name: Sibling set against Vasicek and Ho-Lee
selectors.what: Compare the models on mean reversion, distribution, basis-point volatility and negative rates: Ho-Lee (no mean reversion, normal, constant basis-point volatility), Vasicek (mean reversion, normal, can go negative), CIR (mean reversion, volatility proportional to sqrt(r), non-negative) and the lognormal models (volatility proportional to r).

selectors.name: Shape of the terminal distribution
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Concept of Terminal Distributions' (MR-15 d); revision note: shape of the distribution is 'an important determinant of that model's performance'
selectors.what: Normal, CIR and lognormal models can share the same mean and standard deviation of the rate at a horizon (5% and 2.32% after 10 years in the book) yet differ away from the mean, so out-of-the-money option prices differ significantly.

notSelected: MR-15 a, b, c (Model 3, time-dependent volatility: Vardeez's pointer sits on topic A7's shapes), MR-14 d and f (Ho-Lee and Vasicek calculations: topics A7 and A25) and the reasons why volatility should depend on the rate level (inflation, very low rates) beyond what S3 and S5 need carry no D1 shape.
